faqs.question: What purity grades of sulfuric acid are available for laboratory use in Oman?

faqs.question: What safety precautions are required when handling sulfuric acid in an Oman laboratory?
faqs.answer: Sulfuric acid is one of the most dangerous common laboratory chemicals, with unique hazards: it is strongly corrosive (pH<1 at dilute concentrations), generates intense heat on dilution with water (always add acid to water, never water to acid), and concentrated sulfuric acid dehydrates organic materials (including human tissue) causing severe chemical burns with delayed pain onset. For dilution, always add concentrated acid slowly to water while stirring, never the reverse. description: High-purity potassium chloride for buffer preparation and electrophysiology.

details.longDescription:
Potassium chloride (KCl, CAS 7447-40-7) is a neutral salt, supplied here as a laboratory grade of 99.5% minimum purity, low in sodium and heavy metals, as a white crystalline powder in 500 g, 1 kg and 5 kg packs for research, university, hospital, pharmaceutical and environmental laboratories.

Much of its laboratory use is electrochemical. Potassium and chloride ions move through solution at almost the same speed, so a KCl solution creates only a very small liquid-junction potential, which is why it fills salt bridges and reference electrodes. Silver/silver chloride reference electrodes and combination pH electrodes are usually filled with 3 M KCl saturated with silver chloride, calomel electrodes with saturated KCl, and pH electrodes are stored wet in 3 M KCl. KCl solutions are also the reference standards for conductivity: 0.01 M reads about 1,413 µS/cm at 25 °C and 0.1 M about 12.9 mS/cm. For standards, dry the salt at 105–110 °C and cool it in a desiccator before weighing.

In biology and biochemistry it is a component of phosphate-buffered saline, Ringer's and other physiological solutions, protein purification buffers and microbiology media; electrophysiology uses it in pipette solutions and, at 3 M, to fill sharp microelectrodes. It also serves as an ionic-strength adjuster in potentiometric and ion-selective electrode work. The laboratory grade differs from the site's potassium chloride for drilling fluids (99%, in 25 kg and 50 kg bags) and its muriate of potash fertiliser (60% K2O) in purity, impurity limits and pack size. For cell culture, check the lot certificate of analysis against your method. The laboratory chemicals guide linked on this page lists the other analytical salts.

Handling and storage: potassium chloride is not classified as hazardous under GHS and is not regulated as dangerous goods for transport. Swallowing large amounts can raise blood potassium to dangerous levels, and the dust irritates the eyes mechanically; safety glasses, gloves and a lab coat are enough for routine work. It picks up a little moisture, so keep the container closed in a dry place. Keep it away from strong oxidising agents; hot concentrated sulphuric acid releases hydrogen chloride from it.

It is supplied in 500 g, 1 kg and 5 kg packs. Ask for the certificate of analysis and safety data sheet with your quote, and if your method calls for a particular specification, such as ACS reagent, state it together with pack size and quantity.

title: Magnesium Sulfate (Laboratory Grade)
description: High-purity magnesium sulfate for drying, cell culture, and molecular biology.

details.longDescription:
Magnesium sulphate (MgSO4) is supplied as a laboratory grade in two forms: anhydrous magnesium sulphate (CAS 7487-88-9, 120.37 g/mol), a white powder used mainly as a drying agent, and magnesium sulphate heptahydrate (Epsom salt, MgSO4·7H2O, CAS 10034-99-8, 246.47 g/mol), colourless to white crystals used in media, buffers and solutions. Both are 99% minimum purity and come in 500 g, 1 kg and 5 kg containers for organic chemistry, microbiology, biochemistry, agricultural and teaching laboratories.

Anhydrous magnesium sulphate is the standard drying agent for organic extracts after an aqueous work-up. It takes up water quickly and in quantity by forming hydrates: add it in portions until fresh powder stays free-flowing instead of clumping, then filter it off. It dries faster and more completely than anhydrous sodium sulphate, but it is a fine powder that has to be filtered rather than decanted, and it is slightly acidic, so very acid-sensitive compounds are better dried over sodium sulphate. The heptahydrate has no drying capacity; only the anhydrous form works for this.

The heptahydrate is the usual magnesium source in microbiological and biochemical recipes: M9 minimal medium and the SOB and SOC media used for bacterial transformation, cell culture media formulations, and enzyme assays that need Mg2+ as a cofactor; some proofreading DNA polymerases, such as Pfu, use magnesium sulphate rather than magnesium chloride in their reaction buffer. It is also used in plant nutrition and soil studies in agricultural research. When a recipe names one form and you hold the other, convert by molar mass: 1.00 g of anhydrous MgSO4 corresponds to 2.05 g of the heptahydrate, which is 51% water by mass.

Handling and storage: magnesium sulphate is generally not classified as hazardous under GHS in either form and is not regulated for transport, but the dust can irritate the eyes and respiratory tract, so wear safety glasses and gloves and avoid raising dust. Anhydrous magnesium sulphate is hygroscopic and gives off heat when it meets water; keep the container tightly closed and dry, or it loses its drying capacity. The heptahydrate gradually loses water in warm, dry air, which changes its magnesium content per gram, so keep it sealed as well. Store both away from strong oxidising agents.

Both forms are supplied in 500 g, 1 kg and 5 kg containers with a certificate of analysis and safety data sheet. State the form (anhydrous or heptahydrate), pack size and quantity when you ask for a quote; if your method calls for the ACS reagent specification or nuclease-free testing, ask for the lot certificate of analysis with the quote.

title: EDTA Disodium Salt (Laboratory Grade)
description: High-purity EDTA for chelation, buffer preparation, and molecular biology.

details.longDescription:
EDTA disodium salt dihydrate (Na2EDTA·2H2O, C10H14N2Na2O8·2H2O, CAS 6381-92-6, formula weight 372.24) is the laboratory chelating agent that binds calcium, magnesium, iron and other metal ions into stable complexes. Global Chemicals LLC supplies it at 99% minimum purity, DNase- and RNase-free, as a white crystalline powder in 100 g, 500 g and 1 kg containers, from stock in Muscat, with a certificate of analysis and safety data sheet for every lot.

Analytical use. Disodium EDTA is the titrant of complexometric titration: a 0.01 M solution titrated against Eriochrome Black T at pH 10 measures total hardness, and 1 mL of 0.01 M EDTA corresponds to 1 mg of calcium carbonate. Oman's water-quality laboratories use it for drinking water, irrigation water, boiler feedwater and cooling-tower water; industrial QC labs use it for calcium in cement and gypsum and for metal determinations, and it is used as a protecting agent against chemical interferences in atomic-absorption work. Environmental labs use it to mobilise heavy metals for analysis.

Molecular biology use. EDTA inhibits metal-dependent nucleases, so it protects DNA and RNA in extraction, storage and electrophoresis. The standard 0.5 M stock is made by dissolving 186.1 g of the dihydrate per litre while raising the pH to 8.0 with sodium hydroxide; the salt does not dissolve fully until the pH reaches about 8. From that stock come TE buffer (10 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA), TAE and TBE running buffers, enzyme storage buffers and protein-purification buffers. EDTA salts are also the anticoagulant in blood-collection tubes (modern tubes use the potassium salts K2EDTA or K3EDTA), and disodium EDTA is a stabiliser in biological media.

A 1% solution has a pH of 4–6; the powder is stable for years when kept dry and closed. It is harmful if inhaled as dust and may affect the respiratory tract on repeated exposure (EU CLP H332, H373), so weigh it with dust control, gloves and safety glasses. title: Tris Base (Laboratory Grade)
description: High-purity Tris for buffer preparation and molecular biology applications.

details.longDescription:
Tris base (tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane, tromethamine, THAM, C4H11NO3, CAS 77-86-1, molecular weight 121.14 g/mol) is a white crystalline powder of 99.8% minimum purity, used as a buffering agent in molecular biology, biochemistry, clinical and teaching laboratories. It is supplied in 100 g, 500 g and 1 kg containers.

Its pKa is about 8.1 at 25 °C, so it buffers between roughly pH 7.0 and 9.0. Tris-HCl buffers are made by dissolving the base and titrating it with hydrochloric acid to the target pH. Tris is the buffer in TE (10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 8.0) for storing DNA, in TAE and TBE for agarose gel electrophoresis of nucleic acids, in Tris–glycine SDS-PAGE running buffer (25 mM Tris, 192 mM glycine, 0.1% SDS) and in Towbin transfer buffer for Western blotting (25 mM Tris, 192 mM glycine, 20% methanol, normally without SDS). It also goes into DNA and RNA extraction and cell lysis buffers, PCR reaction buffers and enzyme assays.

Three properties catch people out. The pH of a Tris buffer falls by about 0.03 units for every 1 °C rise, so set the pH at the temperature the buffer will be used: a buffer adjusted to pH 8.0 at 25 °C reads about 8.6 at 4 °C and about 7.7 at 37 °C. Its primary amine reacts with aldehydes and with amine-reactive reagents such as NHS esters, and it interferes with some protein assays, so another buffer is needed for those steps. And Tris reacts with silver ions and can foul the junction of some silver/silver chloride reference electrodes, so use a pH electrode suited to Tris buffers. Dried Tris is also a primary standard for acids, used to standardise hydrochloric acid solutions such as the laboratory hydrochloric acid in this range.

Handling and storage: safety data sheets differ: some classify Tris base as causing skin, eye and respiratory irritation (H315, H319, H335), others list it as not classified; it is not regulated as dangerous goods for transport. Weigh it out without raising dust, wearing gloves and safety glasses, and use a dust mask for larger quantities. Keep the container tightly closed in a cool, dry place, away from strong oxidising agents and strong acids. Filter or autoclave buffer solutions for biological use and store them cold to slow microbial growth.

Tris base is held in stock in Muscat and supplied in 100 g, 500 g and 1 kg containers with a certificate of analysis for each lot and a safety data sheet, with GCC delivery in 2–7 days. If your work needs a molecular-biology grade tested free of DNase, RNase and protease, or a 5 kg pack, ask for the lot certificate and pack options with your quote.

title: Sodium Thiosulfate (Laboratory Grade)
description: High-purity sodium thiosulfate for titrations and analytical chemistry.

details.longDescription:
Laboratory-grade sodium thiosulfate (sodium thiosulphate pentahydrate, Na2S2O3·5H2O, CAS 10102-17-7) is a colourless crystalline reagent at 99.5% minimum purity to ACS specification, supplied by Global Chemicals LLC from stock in Muscat in 500 g, 1 kg and 5 kg containers, with standardised 0.1 N and 0.01 N solutions on request. Every lot ships with a certificate of analysis and safety data sheet; the technical liquid grade for plant dechlorination is listed under oilfield chemicals.

The titrant of iodometry. Thiosulfate reduces iodine to iodide quantitatively, so every oxidant that liberates iodine from potassium iodide is measured with it: free and total chlorine and hypochlorite assay, bromine, hydrogen peroxide and persulphate, copper, and dissolved oxygen by the Winkler method, which water, aquaculture and environmental laboratories across Oman still run beside their electrodes. The end point is the disappearance of the blue starch-iodine colour. Thiosulfate is not a primary standard; standardise the solution against potassium iodate or potassium dichromate, and make it up in freshly boiled, cooled water with a little sodium carbonate or borax as preservative, kept in an amber bottle, because carbon dioxide, bacteria and light slowly decompose it.

Sample preservation. Microbiology laboratories put thiosulfate in sample bottles before sterilising them, about 0.1 mL of a 3% solution per 120 mL bottle, so the chlorine residual in a treated-water sample is destroyed at the moment of sampling and does not keep killing bacteria on the way to the laboratory, which would give false-negative coliform results. Analytical laboratories use it the same way to quench chlorine before organic analysis, and photographic and silver-recovery work uses it as the fixing salt.

Handling and storage: sodium thiosulfate is not hazardous. The pentahydrate effloresces in dry air and cakes in humid air, so keep containers tightly closed; it reacts with acids to release sulphur dioxide, so store it apart from them. Weigh it with clean spatulas and dissolve in distilled water.

title: Phenolphthalein Indicator
description: High-purity phenolphthalein indicator for acid-base titrations.

details.longDescription:
Phenolphthalein (C20H14O4, CAS 77-09-8) is the classic acid–base indicator, supplied here as a ready-to-use 1% solution in ethanol in 100 mL and 500 mL dropper bottles, and as powder or tablets for making up fresh solution, for teaching, water-testing, food, pharmaceutical and industrial quality-control laboratories. The CAS number refers to phenolphthalein itself; the solution is mostly ethanol (CAS 64-17-5).

It is colourless below about pH 8.2 and turns pink to magenta by about pH 10. That range lies on the alkaline side of neutral, which makes it the indicator for titrating weak acids with a strong base, where the equivalence point falls at about pH 8–9: acetic acid in vinegar, citric and lactic acid in juices and dairy products (titratable acidity), the acid value and free fatty acids of oils, and the standardisation of sodium hydroxide against potassium hydrogen phthalate. It also gives a sharp endpoint in strong acid–strong base titrations. Use 2–3 drops per 50 mL titration. Near the endpoint a faint pink can fade as the solution absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, so take the first pink that persists for about 30 seconds; in strongly alkaline solution, above about pH 13, the colour also fades slowly to colourless.

In water analysis it defines phenolphthalein alkalinity (P alkalinity): titration with acid to pH 8.3, which measures hydroxide plus half the carbonate, before titrating on to about pH 4.5 for total alkalinity. The same two-stage titration, with methyl orange as the second indicator (Warder method), analyses mixtures of sodium hydroxide and sodium carbonate in caustic soda. Sprayed on a freshly broken concrete surface it shows the depth of carbonation: sound, alkaline concrete turns pink and carbonated concrete stays colourless. Methyl orange and bromothymol blue, for the acid and neutral ranges, are listed on this site with the other indicators. Phenolphthalein was once used as a laxative but has been withdrawn from that use over cancer concerns.

Handling and storage: because of its ethanol the 1% solution is a highly flammable liquid that causes serious eye irritation (H225, H319), and it travels as Class 3 dangerous goods, usually as UN 1170 (ethanol solution). Phenolphthalein itself is classified in the EU as suspected of causing genetic defects, may cause cancer and suspected of damaging fertility (H341, H350, H361f); a 1% solution is at or above the CLP concentration limits for H341 (1%) and H350 (0.1%), so it carries both as well. Check the safety data sheet supplied with the lot, avoid skin contact and never pipette by mouth; wear gloves, safety glasses and a lab coat. Keep the bottle tightly closed, away from light, heat, flames and strong oxidisers.

It is supplied with a certificate of analysis and a safety data sheet. If your method specifies a particular indicator grade or concentration, such as ACS or 0.1%, state it with your quote.

technicalSpecs: Hazard (1% in ethanol): H225, H319, H341, H350; UN 1170, Class 3

description: High-purity bromothymol blue indicator for neutral pH range titrations.

details.longDescription:
Bromothymol blue (BTB, bromthymol blue, C27H28Br2O5S, CAS 76-59-5) is a sulphonephthalein pH indicator that changes from yellow below pH 6.0 to blue above pH 7.6, passing through green near pH 7. It is supplied as a ready-to-use 0.04% solution in 100 mL and 500 mL bottles and as a powder, for teaching, analytical, microbiology and water-testing laboratories.

Because its colour change brackets pH 7, it is a suitable indicator for strong acid–strong base titrations, where the equivalence point is close to neutral. For a weak acid titrated with a strong base (end point near pH 8–9) phenolphthalein is the better choice, and for a weak base titrated with a strong acid, methyl orange or methyl red. A few drops of the 0.04% solution are enough for one titration. In water and environmental work it is used for colorimetric pH checks in the near-neutral range, including aquarium, aquaculture and soil test kits.

In biology teaching it shows carbon dioxide uptake and release: CO2 from respiration turns a blue or green solution yellow as carbonic acid forms, and photosynthesising aquatic plants remove the CO2 and turn it back. In microbiology it is the pH indicator in differential media such as BTB lactose agar, on which lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacteria produce acid and grow as yellow colonies, while non-fermenters stay blue; it is also used to follow the pH of biological buffer systems. The powder is for laboratories that prepare their own indicator solutions or media; the 0.04% solution saves weighing a few milligrams for each batch.

Handling and storage: bromothymol blue powder is generally not classified as hazardous under GHS, and neither is the dilute aqueous solution, but avoid breathing the dust and wear safety glasses and gloves, because it stains skin and clothing. Indicator solutions made up in ethanol are flammable: keep them away from heat and ignition sources, and check the safety data sheet for the solvent of the solution you buy. Store bottles tightly closed at room temperature, out of direct sunlight and away from strong oxidising agents; an open bottle absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, which shifts the colour of the solution towards yellow.

details.longDescription:
Bacteriological agar (CAS 9002-18-0) is the purified polysaccharide extracted from red seaweed that sets microbiological culture media into a firm, clear gel that bacteria cannot digest. Those numbers are what the laboratory relies on. The usual concentration is 15 g/L (1.5%); 7–10 g/L gives a soft motility or semi-solid medium and 20 g/L a firm surface for streaking. Dissolve the powder by boiling with stirring before autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes; repeated re-melting weakens the gel, so melt only what will be poured.
